content: Severe fatigue is a frequent and debilitating late effect observed in survivors of childhood cancer. While treatment strategies for childhood cancer have improved significantly, leading to higher survival rates, the long-term consequences of cancer and its treatment often persist. Many survivors experience late effects, with severe fatigue being one of the most common and impactful issues. Although most research on fatigue has focused on adult-onset cancer survivors, this review specifically examines fatigue in individuals treated for childhood cancer. The primary objective of this review was to estimate the prevalence of severe fatigue in childhood cancer survivors. Secondary objectives included describing the progression of severe fatigue over time and identifying potential risk factors or associated factors contributing to fatigue. To achieve this, a comprehensive search was conducted across multiple databases, including the Cochrane Central Register of Controlled Trials, MEDLINE/PubMed, and Embase/Ovid, covering studies published up to March 2019. Additional sources, such as reference lists and conference proceedings, were also reviewed. The inclusion criteria for this review encompassed observational studies, randomized controlled trials, and controlled clinical trials that reported on fatigue in childhood cancer survivors. Case series and case reports were excluded. Data extraction and risk of bias assessments were performed independently by two reviewers. When prevalence data for severe fatigue were not explicitly reported, study authors were contacted for further information. A total of 30 studies, involving 18,682 participants, were included in the review. Of these, 18 studies addressed the primary objective of estimating the prevalence of severe fatigue, while 22 studies contributed to the secondary objectives. The studies varied significantly in terms of cancer diagnosis, treatment types, participant age, fatigue assessment methods, and sample sizes. All included studies had at least one item rated as unclear or high risk of bias. Due to the clinical and statistical heterogeneity observed across studies, meta-analysis was not feasible, and results were presented descriptively. The prevalence of severe fatigue among childhood cancer survivors ranged widely, from 0% to 61.7%, across the 18 studies that reported this outcome. In a subgroup of three studies focusing on children aged up to 18 years at the time of fatigue assessment (268 survivors), prevalence rates ranged from 6.7% to 12.5%. In contrast, a subgroup of 12 studies involving participants aged 16 years and older (13,952 survivors) reported prevalence rates ranging from 4.4% to 61.7%. Among survivors of hematological cancers, seven studies reported prevalence rates ranging from 1.8% to 35.9% (1,907 survivors). For brain cancer survivors, two studies (252 survivors) reported prevalence rates of 14.6% and 21.1%. One study involving bone cancer survivors (17 participants) reported a prevalence of 0.0%. Four studies provided prevalence rates of severe fatigue in control groups, including siblings or population-based controls, which ranged from 3.1% to 10.3%. In these studies, childhood cancer survivors were more likely to experience fatigue compared to controls, although the difference was statistically significant in only two studies. The review also examined risk factors and factors associated with fatigue, but the findings were inconsistent due to heterogeneity in study designs and definitions of the factors under investigation. Depression was identified as a potential factor associated with fatigue, while age at diagnosis and education level did not appear to have a significant association. However, due to the lack of meta-analysis, no overall risk estimates could be calculated for any of the reported factors. One study provided longitudinal data on the course of fatigue over time. It found that, over a period of 2.7 years, 31.4% of participants (32 out of 102) reported persistent severe fatigue. The authors concluded that the exact prevalence of severe fatigue among childhood cancer survivors remains unclear due to the significant heterogeneity and methodological limitations of the included studies. Similarly, the progression of severe fatigue over time and the strength of associations with potential risk factors are not well understood. Despite these limitations, the review offers a comprehensive summary of the existing literature on severe fatigue in childhood cancer survivors, highlighting the need for further high-quality research to better understand and address this important issue.
